entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a continuous-time signal from $x(t)$ to $x(-t)$ by mapping every time location $t_0$ to $-t_0$ and recognizing reversal as negative time scaling in the time-domain operation sequence.

sections.section_title: Evaluating Values of $x(-t)$ from $x(t)$

prompt_blocks.text: A signal is given by the table $x(-4)=8$, $x(-1)=4$, $x(0)=5$, $x(1)=2$, and $x(4)=1$. For $y(t)=x(-t)$, what is $y(4)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Flip the query time first: $y(4)=x(-4)$. The table gives $x(-4)=8$, so $y(4)=8$.

prompt_blocks.text: A signal is given by the table $x(-4)=8$, $x(-1)=4$, $x(0)=5$, $x(1)=2$, and $x(4)=1$. For $y(t)=x(-t)$, what is $y(-1)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Flip the query time first: $y(-1)=x(1)$. The table gives $x(1)=2$, so $y(-1)=2$.

sections.section_title: Mapping Time Locations Under Time Reversal

prompt_blocks.text: A signal has labeled features at $t=-2$, $t=0$, and $t=4$. Which list shows the feature times in $x(-t)$ from left to right?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Time reversal sends each location $t_0$ to $-t_0$. So $-2 \mapsto 2$, $0 \mapsto 0$, and $4 \mapsto -4$. Ordered from left to right, the feature times are $-4$, $0$, and $2$.

prompt_blocks.text: A signal has labeled features at $t=-5$, $t=-1$, $t=3$, and $t=7$. Which list shows the feature times in $x(-t)$ from left to right?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Under time reversal, each label changes sign and the values stay attached to the same features. The times become $5$, $1$, $-3$, and $-7$, which ordered from left to right gives $-7$, $-3$, $1$, $5$.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Time Reversal as Scaling by $-1$

prompt_blocks.text: Which description best matches the transformation from $x(t)$ to $x(-t)$?

choice_blocks.text: Time scaling by $-1$, which mirrors the signal across $t=0$.
A shift to the right by $1$.
Amplitude inversion, where the signal values are multiplied by $-1$.
Time scaling by $1$, so the graph stays the same.
Time stretching by a positive factor.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The minus sign is inside the time argument, so it acts on time, not amplitude. That means every time location is multiplied by $-1$ and reflected about $t=0$.

prompt_blocks.text: If a feature is at $t_0=6$ in $x(t)$, where does it appear in $x(-t)$?

choice_blocks.text: At $-6$, because the time coordinate changes sign.
At $6$, because the signal is unchanged.
At $-6$, because the amplitude is inverted.
At $3$, because the time is shifted right by $3$.
At $12$, because the time is stretched by $2$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Time reversal applies the rule $t_0 \to -t_0$. So the feature at $6$ moves to $-6$, and its value stays attached to the same feature.

entries.lesson_core_move: Reflect the graph of $x(t)$ across $t=0$ by moving each feature at time $t_0$ to $-t_0$ while preserving its amplitude.

prompt_blocks.text: The graph below shows $x(t)$ with one isolated peak at $t=4$ and height $2$. Which choice is the reflection across $t=0$, that is, $x(-t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Reflection across $t=0$ changes the time coordinate from $t_0$ to $-t_0$ and keeps the amplitude the same. So the peak moves from $t=4$ to $t=-4$ with height $2$.
That matches Choice $A$.

prompt_blocks.text: The graph below shows $x(t)$ with one isolated peak at $t=1$ and height $3$. Which choice is the reflection across $t=0$, that is, $x(-t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Reflection across $t=0$ moves the peak from $t=1$ to $t=-1$ and keeps the height at $3$. The only change is the sign of the time coordinate.
That matches Choice $D$.

prompt_blocks.text: The graph below shows $x(t)$ with a pulse at $t=-4$ and height $3$, a dip at $t=2$ with depth $1$, and a short flat segment from $t=1$ to $t=3$ at amplitude $2$. Which choice is the full reflection across $t=0$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Reflection across $t=0$ sends each time $t_0$ to $-t_0$ and keeps amplitudes fixed. So the pulse at $t=-4$ moves to $t=4$, the dip at $t=2$ moves to $t=-2$, and the flat segment from $t=1$ to $t=3$ moves to $t=-3$ to $t=-1$. That matches Choice $A$.

prompt_blocks.text: The graph below shows $x(t)$ with a pulse at $t=-1$ and height $1$, a dip at $t=3$ with depth $2$, and a short flat segment from $t=-5$ to $t=-4$ at amplitude $3$. Which choice is the full reflection across $t=0$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Reflection across $t=0$ negates every time coordinate and preserves the amplitudes. So the pulse at $t=-1$ moves to $t=1$, the dip at $t=3$ moves to $t=-3$, and the flat segment from $t=-5$ to $t=-4$ moves to $t=4$ to $t=5$. That matches Choice $A$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a continuous-time piecewise definition $x(t)$ into the correctly ordered interval definition for $x(-t)$ by reflecting each breakpoint across $t=0$ and substituting $-t$ into the segment formulas.

sections.section_title: Reflecting Breakpoints in a Piecewise Signal

prompt_blocks.text: Which breakpoint list gives the left-to-right interval order for $x(-t)$ if $x(t)$ changes formulas at $-2$, $1$, $3$, and $6$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Reflect each breakpoint across $t=0$: $-2 \mapsto 2$, $1 \mapsto -1$, $3 \mapsto -3$, and $6 \mapsto -6$. Then sort the reflected values from left to right to get $-6, -3, -1, 2$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which breakpoint list gives the left-to-right interval order for $x(-t)$ if $x(t)$ changes formulas at $-4$, $-1$, $0$, and $5$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Reflect each breakpoint across $t=0$: $-4 \mapsto 4$, $-1 \mapsto 1$, $0 \mapsto 0$, and $5 \mapsto -5$. Then sort the reflected values from left to right to get $-5, 0, 1, 4$.

sections.section_title: Substituting $-t$ Into Piecewise Segment Formulas

prompt_blocks.text: Which piecewise definition correctly represents $x(-t)$ for a two-piece signal with $3t-1$ on $[-2,1)$ and $4+t$ on $[1,3]$? Keep the reflected interval order from the previous step.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substitute $-t$ into both formulas, then keep the reflected intervals in left-to-right order. The piece from $[1,3]$ becomes $4-t$ on $[-3,-1]$, and the piece from $[-2,1)$ becomes $-3t-1$ on $(-1,2]$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which piecewise definition correctly represents $x(-t)$ for a two-piece signal with $t+2$ on $[-1,2)$ and $3-2t$ on $[2,5]$? Keep the reflected interval order from the previous step.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substitute $-t$ into each segment formula, then write the transformed pieces from left to right. The piece from $[2,5]$ becomes $3+2t$ on $[-5,-2]$, and the piece from $[-1,2)$ becomes $-t+2$ on $(-2,1]$.

sections.section_title: Reordering Reversed Piecewise Intervals

prompt_blocks.text: Which answer choice shows $x(-t)$ in the correct left-to-right order for a three-piece signal with $2t-1$ on $[-6,-3)$, $4$ on $[-3,1)$, and $5-t$ on $[1,4]$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Reflect the intervals first. The rightmost piece on $[1,4]$ becomes the leftmost piece on $[-4,-1]$, the middle piece on $[-3,1)$ becomes $(-1,3]$, and the left piece on $[-6,-3)$ becomes $(3,6]$.
Then write the pieces left to right in the new order: $[-4,-1]$, $(-1,3]$, $(3,6]$. The formulas stay attached to their reflected intervals.

prompt_blocks.text: Which answer choice shows $x(-t)$ in the correct left-to-right order for a four-piece signal with $0$ on $[-5,-2)$, $t+1$ on $[-2,0]$, $3-t$ on $(0,3)$, and $2$ on $[3,6]$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Reflect each interval first. The piece on $[3,6]$ becomes $[-6,-3]$, the piece on $(0,3)$ becomes $(-3,0)$, the piece on $[-2,0]$ becomes $[0,2]$, and the left piece on $[-5,-2)$ becomes $(2,5]$.
Then write the pieces left to right in the new order: $[-6,-3]$, $(-3,0)$, $[0,2]$, $(2,5]$. The formulas follow the intervals after the reflection.

sections.section_title: Reversing a Multi-Interval Piecewise Signal

prompt_blocks.text: Which answer choice gives the complete piecewise definition of $x(-t)$ for the signal below?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Reflect the breakpoints to $[-6,-3]$, $(-3,0]$, $(0,2]$, and $(2,5]$, then substitute $-t$ into each formula. The constant piece stays $-3$, $4-t$ becomes $4+t$, $1$ stays $1$, and $3t-2$ becomes $-3t-2$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which answer choice gives the complete piecewise definition of $x(-t)$ for the signal below?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Reflect the breakpoints to $[-7,-4]$, $(-4,-1]$, $(-1,1]$, and $(1,4]$, then substitute $-t$ into each formula. The last piece $5-2t$ becomes $5+2t$, the constant piece stays $3$, $-t$ becomes $t$, and $2t+1$ becomes $-2t+1$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert an exponential signal $x(t)=Ae^{(\sigma+j\omega)t}$ into $x(-t)=Ae^{-(\sigma+j\omega)t}$ and interpret the result as reversing growth or decay and complex-rotation direction.

sections.section_title: Time Reversal of a Pure Real Exponential

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=2e^{5t}$, which simplified expression equals $x(-t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substitute $-t$ for $t$ to get $x(-t)=2e^{5(-t)}=2e^{-5t}$. The sign in the exponent flips, so the original growth becomes decay as $t$ increases.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=5e^{-2t}$, which simplified expression equals $x(-t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substitute $-t$ for $t$ to get $x(-t)=5e^{-2(-t)}=5e^{2t}$. The exponent changes from negative to positive, so the reversed signal grows as $t$ increases.

sections.section_title: Growth and Decay After Time Reversal

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=3e^{-4t}$, which statement best describes $x(-t)$ as $t$ increases?

choice_blocks.text: It grows exponentially as $t$ increases.
It still decays exponentially as $t$ increases.
It is constant.
It becomes oscillatory.
It stays identical to $x(t)$ as $t$ increases.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Reverse time by replacing $t$ with $-t$.
The exponent becomes positive, so the reversed signal grows as $t$ increases.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=7e^{5t}$, which statement best describes $x(-t)$ as $t$ increases?

choice_blocks.text: It grows exponentially as $t$ increases.
It decays exponentially as $t$ increases.
It is constant.
It becomes oscillatory.
It stays identical to $x(t)$ as $t$ increases.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Reverse time by replacing $t$ with $-t$.
The exponent becomes negative, so the reversed signal decays as $t$ increases.

sections.section_title: Time Reversal of a Pure Complex Exponential

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=e^{j2t}$, which simplified expression is $x(-t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substitute $-t$ into the exponent: $x(-t)=e^{j2(-t)}$. Simplifying gives $x(-t)=e^{-j2t}$. The sign of the imaginary exponent flips, so the phasor rotates in the opposite direction.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=3e^{-j5t}$, which simplified expression is $x(-t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substitute $-t$ into the exponent: $x(-t)=3e^{-j5(-t)}$. Simplifying gives $x(-t)=3e^{j5t}$. The coefficient stays $3$, while the sign of $\omega$ flips and reverses the rotation direction.

sections.section_title: Rotation Direction After Time Reversal

prompt_blocks.text: Let $x(t)=5e^{j4t}$. Which statement best describes the rotation direction of $x(-t)$?

choice_blocks.text: It rotates clockwise.
It rotates counterclockwise.
It rotates in the same direction as $x(t)$.
Its amplitude changes sign, so the rotation direction changes unpredictably.
Only $|\omega|$ changes, so the phasor spins faster after reversal.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substitute $-t$ into the exponential: $x(-t)=5e^{j4(-t)}=5e^{-j4t}$. The sign of $\omega$ flips, so the rotation direction flips from counterclockwise to clockwise.

prompt_blocks.text: Let $x(t)=2e^{-j3t}$. Which statement best describes the rotation direction of $x(-t)$?

choice_blocks.text: It rotates clockwise.
It rotates counterclockwise.
It rotates in the same direction as $x(t)$.
Its amplitude changes sign, so the rotation direction changes unpredictably.
Only $|\omega|$ changes, so the phasor spins faster after reversal.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substitute $-t$ into the exponential: $x(-t)=2e^{-j3(-t)}=2e^{j3t}$. The sign of $\omega$ flips, so the reversed signal rotates counterclockwise.

sections.section_title: Time Reversal of a General Complex Exponential

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=5e^{(-3+j2)t}$, which option gives $x(-t)$ and the correct combined behavior?

choice_blocks.text: $5e^{(3-j2)t}$; amplitude grows and rotation reverses from counterclockwise to clockwise.
$5e^{(3+j2)t}$; amplitude grows and rotation stays counterclockwise.
$5e^{(-3-j2)t}$; amplitude decays and rotation becomes clockwise.
$-5e^{(3-j2)t}$; amplitude grows and rotation reverses from counterclockwise to clockwise.
$5e^{(-3+j2)t}$; amplitude decays and rotation stays counterclockwise.

questions.correct_answer: $5e^{(3-j2)t}$; amplitude grows and rotation reverses from counterclockwise to clockwise.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Time reversal means replacing $t$ with $-t$ everywhere in the exponent, so both signs flip together.
The real part changes from $-3$ to $3$, so decay becomes growth, and the imaginary part changes from $2$ to $-2$, so the rotation direction flips from counterclockwise to clockwise.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=3e^{(4-j5)t}$, which option gives $x(-t)$ and the correct combined behavior?

choice_blocks.text: $3e^{(-4+j5)t}$; amplitude decays and rotation reverses from clockwise to counterclockwise.
$3e^{(-4-j5)t}$; amplitude decays and rotation stays clockwise.
$3e^{(4+j5)t}$; amplitude grows and rotation becomes counterclockwise.
$-3e^{(-4+j5)t}$; amplitude decays and rotation reverses from clockwise to counterclockwise.
$3e^{(4-j5)t}$; amplitude grows and rotation stays clockwise.

questions.correct_answer: $3e^{(-4+j5)t}$; amplitude decays and rotation reverses from clockwise to counterclockwise.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Again, time reversal replaces $t$ with $-t$ everywhere, so the full exponent changes sign together.
The real part changes from $4$ to $-4$, so growth becomes decay, and the imaginary part changes from $-5$ to $5$, so the rotation direction flips from clockwise to counterclockwise.

entries.lesson_core_move: Map each original signal time point $t_0$ to $t=(t_0-b)/a$ for $x(at+b)$ to interpret the combined shift, scale, and possible reversal of a continuous-time signal.

sections.section_title: Mapping Key Time Points for $x(at+b)$

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ has a peak at $t_0=10$, where does that peak appear in $y(t)=x(2t-4)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the inverse map $t=(t_0+4)/2$. Substituting $t_0=10$ gives $t=(10+4)/2=7$, so the peak appears at $t=7$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ has a zero crossing at $t_0=6$, where does that zero crossing appear in $y(t)=x(2t-4)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the same inverse map $t=(t_0+4)/2$. Substituting $t_0=6$ gives $t=(6+4)/2=5$, so the zero crossing appears at $t=5$.

sections.section_title: Finding the Transformed Support Interval

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[0,8]$ and $y(t)=x(2t-4)$, where is $y(t)$ nonzero?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Solve the inside argument for the original time: $2t-4=t_0$, so $t=(t_0+4)/2$. Then map the endpoints $t_0=0$ and $t_0=8$.
Because the scale factor is positive, the endpoint order stays the same. So the support of $y(t)$ is $[2,6]$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[0,6)$ and $y(t)=x(3t-6)$, where is $y(t)$ nonzero?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Solve the inside argument for the original time: $3t-6=t_0$, so $t=(t_0+6)/3$. Then map the endpoints $t_0=0$ and $t_0=6$.
Because the scale factor is positive, the interval keeps the same order, and the half-open right endpoint stays open. So the support of $y(t)$ is $[2,4)$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Combined Compression and Shift

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[0,6]$ and has landmarks at $t_0=0$, $t_0=3$, and $t_0=6$. For $y(t)=x(3t-3)$, what is the support of $y(t)$, and what happens to the width?

choice_blocks.text: The support is $[0,2]$, and the width is compressed by a factor of $3$ while the whole signal shifts right.
The support is $[1,3]$, and the width stays the same while the whole signal shifts right.
The support is $[1,3]$, and the width is compressed by a factor of $3$ while the whole signal shifts right.
The support is $[0,6]$, and the width is compressed by a factor of $3$ without any shift.
The support is $[3,1]$, and the signal is reversed and compressed by a factor of $3$.

questions.correct_answer: The support is $[1,3]$, and the width is compressed by a factor of $3$ while the whole signal shifts right.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set $t_0=3t-3$, so $t=(t_0+3)/3$. Then $t_0=0,3,6$ map to $t=1,2,3$, so the support is $[1,3]$.
The original width is $6$ and the new width is $2$, so the signal is compressed by a factor of $3$ while shifting right.

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[2,12]$ and has landmarks at $t_0=2$, $t_0=7$, and $t_0=12$. For $y(t)=x(2t-4)$, what is the support of $y(t)$, and what happens to the width?

choice_blocks.text: The support is $[2,7]$, and the width is compressed by a factor of $2$ while the whole signal shifts right.
The support is $[3,8]$, and the width stays the same while the whole signal shifts right.
The support is $[1,6]$, and the width is compressed by a factor of $2$ while the whole signal shifts left.
The support is $[3,8]$, and the width is compressed by a factor of $2$ while the whole signal shifts right.
The support is $[8,3]$, and the signal is reversed and compressed by a factor of $2$.

questions.correct_answer: The support is $[3,8]$, and the width is compressed by a factor of $2$ while the whole signal shifts right.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set $t_0=2t-4$, so $t=(t_0+4)/2$. Then $t_0=2,7,12$ map to $t=3,5.5,8$, so the support is $[3,8]$.
The original width is $10$ and the new width is $5$, so the signal is compressed by a factor of $2$ while shifting right.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Combined Expansion and Shift

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[1,5]$ and let $y(t)=x(0.5t-1)$. Where is $y(t)$ nonzero, and what happens to its width?

choice_blocks.text: $[4,12]$; the signal shifts right and expands, so the width doubles to $8$.
$[3,7]$; the signal shifts right, but the width stays $4$.
$[4,12]$; the signal shifts right and compresses, so the width stays $4$.
$[1,5]$; the signal stays in place, so the width stays $4$.
$[-12,-4]$; the signal shifts left and expands, so the width doubles to $8$.

questions.correct_answer: $[4,12]$; the signal shifts right and expands, so the width doubles to $8$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set the inside argument equal to the original time: $t_0=0.5t-1$. Solving gives $t=2(t_0+1)$.
Then $t_0=1$ maps to $t=4$ and $t_0=5$ maps to $t=12$, so the support is $[4,12]$. Because $0.5<1$, the signal expands and the width doubles from $4$ to $8$.

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[0,6]$ and let $y(t)=x(0.25t-2)$. Where is $y(t)$ nonzero, and what happens to its width?

choice_blocks.text: $[2,8]$; the signal shifts right, but the width stays $6$.
$[8,32]$; the signal shifts right and expands, so the width quadruples to $24$.
$[8,32]$; the signal shifts right and compresses, so the width stays $6$.
$[0,6]$; the signal stays in place, so the width stays $6$.
$[-32,-8]$; the signal shifts left and expands, so the width quadruples to $24$.

questions.correct_answer: $[8,32]$; the signal shifts right and expands, so the width quadruples to $24$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set the inside argument equal to the original time: $t_0=0.25t-2$. Solving gives $t=4(t_0+2)$.
Then $t_0=0$ maps to $t=8$ and $t_0=6$ maps to $t=32$, so the support is $[8,32]$. Because $0.25<1$, the signal expands by a factor of $4$ and the width goes from $6$ to $24$.

sections.section_title: Handling Negative Scale Factors in $x(at+b)$

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[0,4]$, where is $y(t)=x(-2t+6)$ nonzero? Give the interval in increasing order.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set the original time equal to the inside argument, so $t_0=-2t+6$. Solving for $t$ gives $t=(6-t_0)/2$.
The endpoints $t_0=0$ and $t_0=4$ map to $t=3$ and $t=1$, so the interval must be written in increasing order as $[1,3]$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[0,8]$, where is $y(t)=x(-4t+16)$ nonzero? Give the interval in increasing order.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set the original time equal to the inside argument, so $t_0=-4t+16$. Solving for $t$ gives $t=(16-t_0)/4$.
The endpoints $t_0=0$ and $t_0=8$ map to $t=4$ and $t=2$, so the interval is reversed and must be written as $[2,4]$.

sections.section_title: Sequencing a Shift and Positive Time Scale

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ has a peak at $t_0=6$, where does that peak appear in $y(t)=x(3(t-2))$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the factored argument first. Set the inside equal to the original peak time and solve for $t$.
So the peak moves to $t=4$. The factor $3$ acts before the shift by $2$ is read from the parentheses.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ has a zero crossing at $t_0=12$, where does that crossing appear in $y(t)=x(4(t+1))$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the same factor-first rule. Match the inside argument to the original crossing time and solve for $t$.
So the crossing appears at $t=2$. The time scale is $4$, then the graph is shifted left by $1$.

sections.lesson_title: Order of Operations in Signal Transformations
sections.section_title: Sequencing a Shift and Time Reversal

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ has a peak at $t_0=10$, where does that peak appear in $y(t)=x(-2(t-1))$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the minus sign first: it reverses time before the shift is read. Then solve the inside argument for the peak location.
So the peak appears at $t=-4$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ has a peak at $t_0=9$, where does that peak appear in $y(t)=x(-3(t-2))$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The negative factor means the time axis reverses before the shift is read. Solve the inside argument for the peak location.
So the peak appears at $t=-1$.

sections.lesson_title: Order of Operations in Signal Transformations
sections.section_title: Factoring an Unfactored Time Argument Before Transforming

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[0,6]$ and $y(t)=x(3t-3)$, what is the support of $y(t)$ after factoring the argument?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Factor first: $3t-3=3(t-1)$.
Then use the inverse map $t=(t_0+3)/3$. It sends $t_0=0$ to $t=1$ and $t_0=6$ to $t=3$, so the support is $[1,3]$.
The correct order is scale by $3$, then shift right by $1$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[2,8]$ and $y(t)=x(2t-4)$, what is the support of $y(t)$ after factoring the argument?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Factor first: $2t-4=2(t-2)$.
Then use the inverse map $t=(t_0+4)/2$. It sends $t_0=2$ to $t=3$ and $t_0=8$ to $t=6$, so the support is $[3,6]$.
The correct order is scale by $2$, then shift right by $2$.

Shift right by $1$ first, then scale by $3$.
Scale by $3$ first, then shift left by $1$.
Scale by $2$ first, then shift right by $1$.
Shift right by $1$ only.

questions.correct_answer: Scale by $3$ first, then shift right by $1$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The support shrinks from width $9$ to width $3$, so the time axis was compressed by $3$ before the shift. That puts the peak at $t=3$ and matches the map $t=t_0/3+1$.
So the correct order is scale by $3$ first, then shift right by $1$.

prompt_blocks.text: The plots below show $x(t)$ and $y(t)$. Use the peak and support locations to identify which sequence of operations produced $y(t)$.

choice_blocks.text: Shift left by $1$ first, then scale by $2$.
Scale by $2$ first, then shift left by $1$.
Scale by $2$ first, then shift right by $1$.
Scale by $3$ first, then shift left by $1$.
Shift left by $1$ only.

questions.correct_answer: Scale by $2$ first, then shift left by $1$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The support shrinks from width $8$ to width $4$, so the time axis was compressed by $2$ before the shift. That puts the peak at $t=2$ and matches the map $t=t_0/2-1$.
So the correct order is scale by $2$ first, then shift left by $1$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which graph matches $y(t)=x(2(t-2))$, meaning scale by $2$ and then shift right by $2$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Scaling by $2$ compresses the source first, so the peak at $t=6$ moves to $t=3$ and the support $[0,12]$ becomes $[0,6]$. Shifting right by $2$ then gives support $[2,8]$ and peak $5$. The opposite order lands at $[1,7]$ with peak $4$, so it is not the correct graph.

prompt_blocks.text: Which graph matches $y(t)=x(3(t+3))$, meaning scale by $3$ and then shift left by $3$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Scaling by $3$ first compresses the source to support $[0,4]$ and peak $2$. Shifting left by $3$ then gives support $[-3,1]$ and peak $-1$. The opposite order lands at $[-1,3]$ with peak $1$, so choice $E$ is the only match.
